There are different views on this topic.

**Ravi Menon** and **Claire Dubois** think that raising pre-seed money is acceptable, with **Claire Dubois** even suggesting raising as early as possible.

**Jonah Whitfield**, on the other hand, advises against raising pre-seed money until reaching at least $10K in monthly recurring revenue, citing the importance of having revenue to attract investors and avoid paying for "selling a story".

There are two views on this topic.

One view is that a generalist should be hired first, as stated by Felix Brandt, who found that a generalist can adapt to changing needs and can handle a variety of tasks. Felix's generalist has been with the company for three years and now runs operations.

The other view is that a specialist should be hired first, as stated by Yuki Tanaka, who believes that hiring a specialist in the area where the founder is weakest can lead to faster progress and better results. Yuki hired a generalist first and later hired a senior engineer, who was able to rebuild and improve the product.

The community is divided on this issue. Some members, like Nadia Haddad, believe that a generalist who can do a bit of everything would be a good first hire, as it would allow the founder to learn and grow alongside the company. 

On the other hand, Yuki Tanaka suggests hiring the strongest specialist in the area the founder is weakest at, which in this case would be a senior engineer. Felix Brandt raises a point that hiring a senior engineer would use up most of the founder's limited runway, and then who would sell the product?

There is no clear consensus on whether a big launch day is better than a quiet launch. Some founders, like Priscilla Ann Moore, suggest that a big launch should only happen when the product is ready and has a certain level of organic usage (at least 10 weekly active users). Others, like Ingrid Solberg, argue that a big launch can bring press and investors, while Mateo Rossi notes that a quiet launch can help filter out non-paying users.

The community is divided on this issue. Some members, like Samir Qureshi, suggest launching with a free tier to get adoption, but with a 14-day trial and no permanent free tier, and then revisiting after three months. Others, like Beatriz Lopes, advise charging from day one and not offering a free tier, as paying customers provide the only real signal.
